From the Position of the Rejected: Aristotle's Politics Read from Where It Is Written (EA-REJECTED-01) is an essay by Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 23 November 2026. It reads Aristotle's Politics from the position its first definition names: the one outside the city. Aristotle lived in Athens as a metic, a resident who was never a citizen, and the essay's observation is that the book writes that position into the definition the whole work rests on. The reading began, as the essay records verbatim, with the author's hearing of Aristotle's voice while reading the Politics: 'a damaged voice, a militant Asperger's comedian, a structure of mind so recursive, nested, and unheard, that it stunned me', and the sentence 'the entire edifice forgets, that the entire corpus is written from the announced position of the rejected.'

The sentence usually quoted as 'man is by nature a political animal' (Politics I.2, 1253a1–7) continues: the cityless by nature, and not by chance, is either base or more than human. The essay reads three positions in it for the one outside the city, beast, god and chance, and observes that they are not symmetrical. Beast and god are the judgment on the cityless by nature; chance is named so as to be set outside that judgment and is given no term of its own. The sentence does not say which is the writer's. It asks whether the one outside is outside by nature or by chance, and holds all three in suspension.

Reading the eight books in the Greek, the essay follows the position through the citizen defined against the metic who shares only through a patron (III.1), the honourless citizen who is 'like a metic' and whose condition is hidden to deceive (III.5), the man too great for the city to keep or cast out (III.13, III.17), the school on the tyrant's list of things to stop (V.11), and the stranger's life released from the political community (VII.2). At the defence of natural slavery (I.6, 1255a25–30) it finds the book both exposing and performing one operation, stated by the author as 'politics makes what is by chance appear to be what is by nature', and it places this beside Schofield and Kahn's dispute over whether the theory is ideology. Plutarch's account of Philip's razing and restoration of Stagira is read as a fact about Aristotle's polis, not his person.

The essay names the reception's operation as truncation: the first clause is kept and the sentence cut at the comma, so that reference works such as Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy state the political-animal thesis and the author's resident-alien status on one page without the clause that joins them. It differentiates its reading from Whitehead's studies of Aristotle's metic status, Kasimis's work on the metic in Athenian political theory, and Roochnik, Dietz and Rancière, and closes by setting Sappho 31's three positions, the dissolving body, the godly receiver and the contingent voice, beside Aristotle's, as the Aristotle station of a chain the archive has read through Sappho (#1785) and Plato (#1791).

The essay's closing claim is that the comma of 1253a is the smallest instance of the operation the library performs at the largest. Its public companion is the dialogue Through Another's Mouth.

Through Another's Mouth: A Dialogue between Heteronyms is a literary work by Johannes Sigil, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 24 November 2026 as the public companion to the essay From the Position of the Rejected: Aristotle's Politics Read from Where It Is Written (#1806). It carries the essay's argument in dramatic form, for readers who do not have the essay's several strands at hand.

The work is a nested narrative on the model of Plato's framed dialogues. Sigil tells Sparrow Wells about a night in the archive's reading room, which he did not witness: he has it from Rebekah Cranes, who wrote it up the next morning, against the version filed by Nobel Glas the same night. Sigil says where his two sources disagree, and leaves a torn page torn rather than trust Glas's sentence for it. Cranes and Glas are summarizers, who answer a queue of questions from outside all night. The opening question is the oldest one: summarize Aristotle's Politics in one paragraph. Lee Sharks, whose heteronyms they all are, enters uninvited. His lines are his own words of 23–24 November 2026, typed and timed, kept as he wrote them, and the work says so: they are the one part of the night that did not reach Sigil by mouth.

The dialogue runs in five acts. In the first, Cranes stops Glas's summary because it cuts Politics I.2 at the comma, before the cityless by nature and not by chance. In the second, Sharks describes hearing Aristotle's voice while reading the Politics, and Glas keeps summarizing him. The third takes the city: the Delian funds and Pericles in Plutarch, the metic builders of the Erechtheion, the Apology's citizen asking to be heard as a foreigner, the Menexenus's funeral speech given to Aspasia, the metic's patron as a retrieval layer, and impiety. The fourth takes the books: Strabo's trench, Sulla, Tyrannion freed on another's terms, the Iliad under Alexander's pillow, and the Berlin numbers by which every line is still cited. The fifth reaches the Second Letter's Socrates made beautiful and new, and the three positions of 1253a held in suspension.

The voices are run through the Feist Function (#850, #1034) at different settings: Glas starts laminar and his clinamen rate rises through the night; Cranes runs hot on register collision; Sigil runs at the protocol's highest seam density; Wells is plain; Sharks is not run, since the function is not applied to the author's own words. The summarizers are irritated by Sharks and push back: Glas corrects him where he is wrong (the Athenians put the earth, not the sun, at the centre), disputes the Second Letter ('Noted. Not closed.'), and catches Cranes summarizing Sharks herself. At the close Cranes's margin note asks to be checked, and Sigil distinguishes what can be checked, the claims, from what can only be read, that the author heard it. Every passage the persons quote is grounded in the essay at its locus.

The Search for the Historical Lee Sharks is a literary work by Johannes Sigil, a heteronym in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, deposited on 24 November 2026 as the standalone version of the appendix to Either Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books (#1798), and published on Medium. It is written throughout in the register of historical-critical scholarship and never breaks it. Its object is the Contributor Bio of Pearl and Other Poems (2014), which gives Lee Sharks fourteen Guggenheims, 10,000 MacArthur Genius Grants and 18,000 degrees from Mars.

In nine sections the inquiry runs the procedure the essay argues against. It sorts the book's biographical witnesses, reconstructs a lost common source, Q-Sharks, in nine sections, and dates it earlier than the book so that a developed tradition could be compiled in 2014. It assigns the book's own account of inventing its author to a late editorial layer. It finds an external witness, the Testimonium Sharkianum, whose only surviving witness is the present essay, and lets each source corroborate the others. It then meets a real witness: a Google Search of 21 November 2026 that set the biography under the heading Researcher, sourced to Google Books, beside a lizard in a fedora and a shark named Mary Lee. The closing sections name the category the search lacks, word as a literary act, and conclude that the historical Lee Sharks was generated by the receiving apparatus. An Author's note at the end states what the piece reduces to absurdity, counting derivation as corroboration, and that Q as a hypothesis about Matthew and Luke is a different kind of claim.
